items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] My name is Monk Rowe and we are filming in Manhattan today and I am very pleased to have, for the second time, my guest Jon Hendricks... [INTERVIEWEE] Thank you very much.

ctx.x: Vocalese master Jon Hendricks celebrated the millennium by revisiting his musical past and creating a legacy for the future. A reunion with Annie Ross at New York’s Blue Note brought rave reviews and a validation of their lasting contribution to American music. Jon is also preparing to launch the first collegiate program to teach the art of vocalese at the University of Toledo. Part II was conducted in New York City by Monk Rowe on January 29, 2000.

My name is Monk Rowe and we are filming in Manhattan today and I am very pleased to have, for the second time, my guest Jon Hendricks, the inventor of vocalese. And I’m going to pin you down momentarily on your definition. And you look great by the way.

items.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] My name is Monk Rowe... [INTERVIEWEE] Thank you, Monk.

ctx.x: Vocalist Jon Hendricks was born in Newark, Ohio in 1921. He has taken the vocalese style of singing pioneered by King Pleasure and Eddie Jefferson to a virtuoso level and is a household name with jazz fans around the world. His unique re-working of Basie standards with Lambert, Hendricks and Ross and later Joe Williams, established a new style of vocal jazz in the late 50s and this trio recorded such classic tunes as “Cloudburst,” “Gimme That Wine” and “Centerpiece.” His production “Evolution of the Blues” became…
